quote: I'm sorry. I can't hear you.
stewart_read: Minor audio/connection friction at the very start required the rep to repeat the intro. Not a rep error, but it ate the first 15+ seconds and slightly softened the opening's legitimacy framing since it had to be restated.
coaching_implication: No action needed — flagging only as color; this is a connection issue, not a rep skill gap.

quote: Okay. Who did you, get installed with?
stewart_read: Rep correctly and immediately runs the orphaned-flow qualifier the moment the customer discloses existing solar, asking who installed it before anything else.
coaching_implication: This is the one clean procedural win on the call — worth naming to the rep as the right instinct so it's reinforced.

quote: Unfortortunately, my company, we're not we're not able to work on another company's, equipment or anything like that. You'd have to, like, probably reach out to, like, another solar contractor
stewart_read: The DQ call itself is correct per policy, but the delivery is hedgy and filler-heavy ('probably', 'like... like...') rather than a clean, confident disqualification-and-redirect. This is a delivery issue riding on top of a correct decision, not a wrong decision.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive stumble on wording vs. a deliberate soft framing to keep the customer friendly — the repeated 'like' and 'probably' reads as unprepared phrasing rather than a strategic softening choice.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to have a clean, one-sentence DQ line ready for this exact scenario (existing system, unsupported installer) so it lands with authority instead of trailing off.

stewart_read: Customer asks a technical efficiency question post-DQ; rep answers with a panel model number instead of redirecting. Since the customer was already disqualified, this isn't costing a sale, but it establishes a pattern of engaging on closer-tier technical content without a redirect reflex.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive — rep is just being polite/conversational with a DQ'd customer who has nothing to lose by chatting; strategic redirect wasn't necessary since no appointment was at stake. This is the stronger read given the customer was already gone as a prospect.
coaching_implication: Even on a dead lead, practicing the escape hatch ('that's exactly what our specialist digs into') keeps the habit sharp for when scope creep actually costs a live deal.

quote: I'm not entirely too sure on the efficiency rating.
stewart_read: Rep admits the gap honestly rather than fabricating a number — this is the correct choice among the three knowledge-gap responses (dodge, admit-and-recover, fabricate). He picked admit, but didn't pair it with a redirect to a specialist.
coaching_implication: Reinforce the honesty; add the missing second half — pairing admission with a bridge line to a specialist even on dead leads keeps the rep's default response consistent across calls.

quote: well, okay. So the actual roofing style is is sometime down the road, I take it.
stewart_read: Customer floats a future need — he'll likely need a roof when his current panels 'go tits up' in ten to fifteen years — and the rep's response ('reach out to us then, a couple years from now') does not capture any contact info, note, or routing; it just tells the customer to call back on his own initiative someday.
alternative_hypothesis: This is a distant, speculative signal (10-15 years out, self-initiated by the customer) rather than an active near-term need, so the rep letting it go with a light response is defensible — there's little to actually route today.
coaching_implication: Worth a light mention to the rep: even on a far-out or DQ'd lead, capturing a one-line note or offering to have someone follow up down the line costs nothing and keeps optionality open, but this is not a costly miss given the timeline involved.
